results.task: Write a Python function to validate AWS S3 bucket names. A valid S3 bucket name must be 3-63 characters long, contain only lowercase letters, numbers, hyphens, and periods, start and end with a letter or number, and cannot contain consecutive periods or hyphens at the start/end.
strengths: The function correctly validates the length requirement (3-63 characters)
Proper type checking to ensure input is a string
Correctly rejects uppercase letters with case-sensitive regex patterns
Properly rejects consecutive periods with the '..' check
Correctly rejects hyphens at the start or end of the bucket name
Comprehensive test suite that covers most edge cases
Allows only lowercase letters, numbers, hyphens, and periods as specified
Correctly rejects underscores and other invalid characters
The logic flow is clear and easy to follow
All regex patterns are appropriate for the requirements
weaknesses: Redundant regex matching - the final check `^[a-z0-9.-]+$` makes the earlier individual character checks partially redundant
The solution performs 5 separate regex operations which could be combined into a single comprehensive regex for better performance
The final regex pattern `^[a-z0-9.-]+$` doesn't explicitly prevent consecutive hyphens, though the task description doesn't explicitly require this check either
No explicit handling or documentation about what happens with None input (though the isinstance check covers it)
Minor inefficiency: checking for '-' at start/end after already validating first/last character are letters/numbers is somewhat redundant
results.reasoning: The solution correctly implements all the stated requirements from the task. It validates bucket name length (3-63 chars), enforces lowercase letters/numbers/hyphens/periods only, requires starting and ending with alphanumeric characters, and rejects consecutive periods. The comprehensive test suite verifies correct behavior for valid cases like 'my-bucket', 'my.bucket', '1bucket' and correctly rejects invalid cases like '-my-bucket', 'my..bucket', 'MY-BUCKET', and 'ab'. The code is readable and handles edge cases well. The main weaknesses are code efficiency issues (multiple regex calls, redundant checks) rather than correctness issues. The solution passes all provided test cases and meets the stated criteria.

results.task: Write a regex pattern to match valid AWS IAM role ARNs. The pattern should match ARNs in the format 'arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:role/ROLE_NAME' where ACCOUNT_ID is 12 digits and ROLE_NAME can contain alphanumeric characters, hyphens, and forward slashes.
strengths: Correctly anchors the pattern with ^ and $ to match the entire string
Properly validates the account ID with exactly 12 digits using \d{12}
Uses the correct AWS ARN prefix 'arn:aws:iam::'
Correctly uses \w to match alphanumeric characters
Includes support for forward slashes with /
The pattern is concise and readable
weaknesses: The character class [\w\-/]+ allows one or more characters, but doesn't validate that ROLE_NAME actually starts with a valid character - while \w includes letters, digits, and underscore, the pattern allows leading underscores which may not be ideal for role names

Does not explicitly prevent matching invalid characters that might be problematic in real AWS role names (e.g., the pattern would match 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/___' which is unlikely to be a valid role name)
The \w character class includes underscores, which while technically valid in role names, is often not mentioned in the requirements
results.reasoning: The regex pattern successfully matches the required format and will correctly validate the test cases provided in the criteria. It will accept valid ARNs like 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/MyRole' and 'arn:aws:iam::999999999999:role/path/to/my-role' while rejecting invalid formats like 'arn:aws:iam::12345:role/test' (wrong account ID length) and 'arn:aws:s3:::bucket/key' (wrong service). The pattern is clean and appropriate for the task. The main limitation is that it's quite permissive with what constitutes a valid ROLE_NAME (e.g., allows sequences like underscores), but this is a minor issue since AWS does permit underscores and the pattern still enforces the structural requirements effectively.
